title: The Medicalising of Sadness
sentences: It has become strangely normal to treat ordinary sadness as a condition requiring a diagnosis.
A bad week at work is reframed as burnout, and a quiet mood becomes a symptom to be managed.
This is not necessarily dishonest, yet it does narrow what counts as an acceptable way to feel.
Wellness culture promises balance, but it often just replaces one demanding standard with another.
To the extent that suffering gets a label, it can be treated, tracked, and, crucially, sold.
And yet something is lost when grief or boredom is folded into the language of disorder.
Ordinary discomfort has always nudged people toward growth, however unwelcome it felt at the time.
Precisely because relief is marketed as constant and available, its absence starts to feel wrong.
Arguably, a person entitled to feel nothing but fine is being quietly denied their own life.
The irony is that chasing wellness so relentlessly can itself become a fresh source of anxiety.
Perhaps the healthier position is to let some sadness simply pass, unnamed and untreated.
